utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if there is nothing else that the parties would like to raise -- yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if there is any news on the waiver issues, whether or not there is going to be a report back about whether or not there were waivers for those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can respond to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Last week we contacted the witnesses and informed them to contact the commission. We also contacted the commission or the secretary of the commission and demanded that they get back to us with some concrete answers. I don't believe that we contacted them yesterday, but today one of the things on the list was to actually contact the witnesses again to ensure that they physically go down to the commission and request something in writing so it would be faxed immediately over here for the Court and for the Prosecution. So that's the update that I have. The only other thing I can say is getting answers, concrete answers, has been rather difficult, so -- but we are working on it in every possible way, and we -- I know that one of the witnesses for sure went there last week and spoke with the secretary or the secretariat of the commission. So -- but as soon as we get out today, or even during the break, I will ask my case manager to -- Mr. Mominov to get on it and follow up on this matter. So we are fully aware of the Prosecution's position, and we fully intend to do everything that we possibly can to expedite this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We believe that we are also expecting an early answer as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, good morning, Witness. I can't hear you. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you now. Before, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: My name is Predrag Drinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: D-r-i-n-i-c diacritic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Drinic, where are you from?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: From Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is, from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, back in July 1995, what position did you hold? What was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I was the military prosecutor of the army of Republika Srpska in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at what level were you the military prosecutor; at the basic level or at the appellate level?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: At the appellate level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to go backwards. First of all, how long had you been with the military prosecution office?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: From 1992 to the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you please tell us, when you started with the military prosecution office, at what position did you start at?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I was in the first instance military prosecution office in Bijeljina, I was a military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when did you advance to become the -- well, advance to the appellate level, first of all?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: In mid-1994. That was when I came to the military prosecutor's office of the army of Republika Srpska as deputy military prosecutor, and on the 9th of September, 1995, I became the military prosecutor -- no. Excuse me. Excuse me. On the 9th of September -- yes, 1995. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So just to make sure I understand, initially you were the deputy prosecutor at the basic level; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I was the chief prosecutor in Bijeljina at the court of first instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then at some point you became the chief prosecutor at the second instance?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, beginning on the 9th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if I understand your earlier testimony, you stayed there in that position until sometime 2000; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 15th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, going even backwards, further back, prior to becoming a military prosecutor, could you please tell us what your occupation was.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I was an attorney-at-law in Modrica from 1986 until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you took your position as the military prosecutor at the first instance, were you qualified?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And briefly, could you please tell us whether the criminal procedure as it existed back then for the civilian courts and for the military courts, were there any differences?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before we go into the specifics, I would like you to please walk us through the process so we have a better understanding of the procedure as it existed back then. First of all, would you please tell us how a case would be initiated at the prosecution level.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: The office of the prosecutor had to receive as an initial document a criminal report. After this, the prosecutor who was in charge of this would evaluate the criminal report and the supporting documents. If there were grounds to suspect that a crime had been committed by a particular individual, the prosecutor would submit to the first instance military court, that is to the investigating judge of that court, a motion to initiate an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. First of all, this criminal report, who would prepare such a report?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: The criminal report in the military was prepared by the military police and the security organ in the units at a certain level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was it possible for an individual to come directly to the -- to the prosecutor of the first instance to file a report?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to the Law on Criminal Procedure, this was possible in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if such an individual did in fact come to the prosecutor of the first instance, would the prosecutor be duty-bound to at least look into the matter?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what if you as the prosecutor deemed it necessary to gather additional information in order to make a determination as to whether there was a suspect and, therefore, forward the case or the file on to the investigative judge? What would you -- who would you rely on to gather that additional information?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I would rely on the military police and the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you say the security organ, and I'm speaking now at the first instance where you indicated you had served as the prosecutor there, what part of the security organ are we speaking of, and where would that security organ be located?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Criminal reports were submitted by units at the brigade level, and it was their security organ who collected additional information to support a criminal report. In that case, one had to keep in mind that it also depended on the rank of the soldier. If the person in question was a high-ranking soldier or belonged to a high-level unit, then information would be requested from the security organ of his unit or a higher-level unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you indicated that you were in Bijeljina, as I understand, when you became a -- when you were the prosecutor at the first instance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for the record, how many first instances -- instance prosecution offices were there, or courts were there, during that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in the RS, I should say, to be more precise?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: There were four first instance military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the one for Bijeljina, what area did that cover?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Mostly the area that belonged to the East Bosnia Corps, as far as territory goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the Drina Corps? Do you know which court handled matters related to the Drina Corps or that -- that area where the Drina Corps was situated and responsible for?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: The court and prosecutor's office in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that if you needed additional information you would go to either the military police or the security organ. Let's assume that you had that additional information and the suspect was identified. Could you then walk us further on to the procedure. What would happen next when the matter went to the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: A motion to initiate an investigation would be submitted to the investigating judge, and the investigating judge, before opening an investigation, would assess whether there was sufficient elements for a crime or, that is, the crime mentioned in the motion to initiate proceedings or an investigation. If in his view there were sufficient elements, that is there were grounds to suspect that the crime had been committed, he would issue a decision on initiating an investigation, and he would carry out the investigation. This means that he would gather evidence to support the fact that this crime had been committed, and he would issue instructions that the evidence proposed by the prosecutor be collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. Who would gather that evidence for the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: If the investigating judge felt it necessary to have other evidence collected, material evidence for the most part, this would be done by the military police and the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And please continue. What would happen -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: After the evidence had been collected, the judge would assess whether this was enough to prove the crime. That is, the investigating judge was independent to a certain extent in collecting evidence for the investigation because he could, on his own initiative, decide whether to gather certain evidence or not. After deciding that he had gathered enough evidence, he would submit the entire file with all the evidence to the prosecutor in charge of the case for further proceedings, which means that the prosecutor would decide whether there were grounds to suspect that the crime had been committed, and he could either issue an indictment, or if he felt that the investigation had not arrived at the desired result, he would drop the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me go back a little bit. When forwarding the matter to the investigative judge, that is after you've gathered additional information if the case required so, would it be possible to keep the name of the complaining witness secret from the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about in gathering the additional information? You indicated that you would need to rely on the military police and the security organ. Could you keep the identity of the person who would be lodging this complaint or this allegation for you to initiate the proceedings, could you keep his identity a secret?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please explain to us why not.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: According to the Law on Criminal Procedure which was in force at the time, the institute of a protected witness did not exist. Besides, every criminal report, in view of the gravity of the crime, if there was a false report this would lead to certain consequences for the person submitting this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Was there a recording process of those who would be submitting criminal complaints or filing criminal reports, however you wish to characterise it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The military prosecutor's office, in its register, had a column in which the name of the person or organ submitting the criminal report was entered, and this was obligatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, would it have been possible to at least keep this register a secret, or at least that portion of the register secret where the name was recorded of the person filing the complaint? So in other words, if the security organ wanted to know who it was that was lodging the complaint, you could keep that information from them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: If someone asked for this information, such as the security organ, no, this could not be concealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: First of all, the law did not provide for this possibility. It did not provide for secrecy. In the register, there was a column indicating who had filed the report, and for the prosecutor to ask the security organ to collect certain information pursuant to the criminal report, the report itself or, rather, a copy of it was delivered, and this would also contain the information as to who had filed it. And also, it was the job of the security organ to know certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's assume that this -- that the matter was rather sensitive. Could you please explain to us what protective measures you would have --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear your entire question. There was an interruption in the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's assume -- can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's assume that the matter was rather sensitive in nature, perhaps even dangerous to the person filing the complaint or providing this information. Could you please explain to us what protective measures you as the prosecutor could afford such an individual or would afford such an individual.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No protective measures. There were no protective measures at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And incidentally, so I don't have to ask you this question later, what sort of protective measures were available to the prosecutors if they wished to proceed with cases where there might be some danger involved?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No, no measures. I had no protective measures and no security at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the judges? Did they have any? I mean, they're a little bit higher than the prosecutor. Surely there must have been something to protect them.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. There was nothing for them either, no form of protection. I do not know that any of the judges ever had any protection or security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go through this guideline, I want to show you what has been marked or has come into evidence as P380.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may have the assistance of the -- Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, if you could please look at this document.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- and tell us whether you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You've seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Indeed I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And for the record, could you please tell us what P380 is.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: This is a document that was submitted to us by the military prosecutor's office attached to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. This document provided certain guidelines for determining criteria for criminal prosecution in cases of certain crimes that were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to focus your attention to a particular paragraph that has been discussed previously in this court. Perhaps you can give us your opinion and shed some light. If I could refer you to page -- I believe it would be 14, paragraph 2, and in our version, the English version, it would be page 8. So for the English version the ERN number would be 00814384. Paragraph -- it's page number 14, sir, paragraph 2. And if you could look at actually the first two paragraphs on page 14, and that would be the first two paragraphs on page number 8 for us. Actually, I'm told, sir, if you go back to page 13, the last paragraph on the previous page. Mr. Drinic, if you went back to page 13, the last paragraph, that's where your version begins.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it, having worked with these guidelines, you are familiar with the guidelines?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please explain to us, what exactly are these paragraphs referring to?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: These paragraphs are about the responsibility of, for the most part, military officers and all soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska in relation to acts that might be committed against the population and that would constitute war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And from these paragraphs, are we to conclude that officers have a responsibility to file complaints against their soldiers, or anyone, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They have the duty to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So -- and was that part of the law, as it were, back then?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was part of the law. This is merely a comment on some of the laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- so it would appear that if an officer were to become aware that one of the members of his unit had committed a crime, that officer would be duty-bound to file a complaint or to -- to initiate a proceeding; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, concretely, perhaps you can help us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I don't believe we need this any more. Well, right now we don't need your assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Concretely, what if at the brigade level, we're speaking of a brigade commander, and what if he were to learn - and this is merely a hypothetical - but what if he were to learn that his chief of intelligence and security, because that person holds both positions, but his chief of intelligence and security had been involved in what would amount to war crimes and he came to you? From your earlier testimony, I take it you would have to record the officer's name, correct, the commander's name?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And specifically in this instance, to whom would you rely -- you would go to in order to proceed with the -- with this case in order to gather, perhaps, more additional information before you could refer the case to the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: If the officer in question was an intelligence and security officer of the same brigade that the officer who came there to file a criminal report belonged to, in order to gather such information as was necessary on the crime, I would forward this to a security organ of a higher level, in this case the corps level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what would you expect them to do at that higher level, at the corps level, that is the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: To gather the necessary information. At any rate, to carry out some of the pre-trial procedures, to collect statements and possibly hard evidence found on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What if the same commander who is reporting on his chief of security were to also tell you, as the prosecutor of the first instance, that the security organ at the corps level was in fact, or suspected of, having been involved as well? Where would you refer the matter then?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I would forward the file to the security organ of the Main Staff, because the Main Staff in that case would be the superior unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what if, in this instance, the hypothetical that I'm working with, the commander were to say, "Well, not only is the chief of security at the brigade level involved and the assistant commander of security at the corps level is involved, but it would appear that the head of security at the Main Staff level, in particular we're speaking of Colonel Beara, was involved, what would you do then? To -- where would you refer this matter to in order to gather additional information to proceed against these individuals?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: In principle, there is no superior unit to the security organ that is attached to the Main Staff. However, for purely practical reasons, I would forward the file to the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the commander of the Main Staff would be Mladic himself?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But is there not in fact someone above Colonel Beara before you get to General Mladic? I'm referring to General Tolimir. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Tolimir, establishment-wise, was indeed Colonel Beara's superior, however, he did not have the sort of service at his disposal that this required. What I needed at the time in order to collect this sort of information was the sort of backing that Colonel Beara had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, speaking of Beara, perhaps you could assist us a little bit. His name has popped up a few times in this trial. First of all, did you know Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in touch with him several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so did you know of him as well, that is of his reputation, if in fact he enjoyed one?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: First of all, I must say that he liked me personally. However, whenever I requested a document from his service, I never got any. As to what I knew about the other soldiers and officers, knowing Beara's rank and knowing the kind of department that he worked for, I know that he was even more respected, or perhaps feared, than would have been usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about the security organ itself? What sort of a reputation did they have?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: By their very nature the security organ - I assume this applies to all armies of the world - the security organ is always an elite unit above other units, with greater authority compared to all other units. To all practical intents and purposes, the security organ had authority to control, to monitor and supervise all the other units, and security organs as a rule were respected by the other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to my hypothetical and I want to put it slightly in a more concrete fashion. Keeping in mind the environment at the time - and we're going back now to 1995 - July and onwards, but 1995, 1996, that period, could you please tell us how realistic would it have been for anyone, let alone a commander, to -- of a brigade, for instance, to initiate a criminal complaint requesting the prosecution to gather information with respect to atrocities that might have been committed or were committed by members of the security organ that go as high as Beara himself?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: In principle, de jure, that would have been possible. However, in view of the kind of environment that we were surrounded by and the atmosphere, the feelings of the citizens, the soldiers, the army officers, this would not have been realistic, or at least such a person would have had to be gravely concerned about the safety and lives of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: These were serious crimes. These were officers or, rather, persons of such a high rank of the Supreme Command body. In principle, these people were, in a way, dangerous. This would have been very risky.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, wouldn't there be a possibility for an anonymous complaint, in other words, for someone to file a complaint by writing without disclosing their identity? Would you not then proceed, you the prosecutor, based on that information?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: There was indeed such a possibility for an anonymous tip-off, a criminal report being filed by mail, for example. Of course this would bear no signature if such a parcel ever arrived. Certainly the prosecutor would evaluate the report, and based on that report, the prosecutor would probably seek further information from one of the security organs. The information requested, however, would be more in order to familiarise the security organ with what the criminal report contained rather than seeking particular information, because this kind of criminal report would always have been viewed as incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- but we're speaking about some fairly serious crimes. Why wouldn't you, for instance, had you been -- had this occurred, why wouldn't you just go ahead and proceed with attempting to gather information? In other words, asking the security organ to gather information of crimes that the organ itself or members of the organ, including their commander, had committed? What's wrong with that? It seems fairly reasonable, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: In principle, that's what this information would contain. If the security organ were in possession of any such information as contained in the criminal report, they'd be expected to submit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How realistic is it under the circumstances during that environment, in light of what we're talking about, the sort of crimes that we're talking about, how realistic would it have been to expect members of the security organ to gather information where they themselves and their officers had been directly involved in? How realistic is that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Well, we can look at any crime in the same way in terms of how realistic this would be, not only this one. I don't believe that any person who has committed a crime would be willing to denounce themselves unless there was another kind of interest at stake. I simply can't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to go back to this -- these guidelines, just to tie up a couple of points based on what we have been discussing right now. If you could go to the last page. Actually -- yeah, the last page. In the English version it would start at the last page of -- or the bottom of the page 8 and go on to page 9. You would have to start, sir, at page 15, page 15, and I believe it goes on to part of 16, and I just want to make sure that what you've told us is consistent with these guidelines. The bottom of page 15, and you would have to go to the next page. It would appear here, sir -- if I can read the appropriate section, if I could focus your attention. It says here at the bottom of page 8 in our version, in our version: "So that the command of the Main Staff has a full understanding of types and number of these criminal offences, all unit commands shall..." First of all, what does that mean, "unit commands"? What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Unit commands would comprise the commander and his assistants who are in charge of certain areas of activity. For example, assistant commander for security would be a member of that team, assistant commander for logistics, assistant commander for morale, and all other tasks and issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So when we're speaking about all unit commands, we're not just speaking about the commandant, the commander himself?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that -- that phrase "unit commands" encompasses his commanders, his komandirs, or his assistant commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So in other words, the commander himself would also be relying on the chief of security in this instance if we're dealing at the brigade level? All right, you have to speak a little louder so we get that on the record.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, it goes down, it says -- it says: "They shall work on uncovering all war crimes against humanity and international law on territory in their area of responsibility." And then if we go down this list, it says: "Inform the closest military police, security and military judicial organs about any crimes they discover." If we go down this list, it continues to mention military police, security, and military judicial organs. So if I understand you correctly, these guidelines validate what you've told us, that it would be the military police, the security organ, the security organ and the judicial organ that would be involved in processing these sorts of cases; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, could you as the military prosecutor, could you bypass the security organ and perhaps go to the military police and have the military police conduct an investigation against the security organ? Because if we look at this document here, it would appear that the military police is separate and not part of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: In principle, the military police are not separate from the security organ. The security organ, for the most part, advises the military police on certain tasks and gives them certain tasks or orders them certain tasks. The lower MP units only have ordinary police officers who do such things as providing security, providing escort, that kind of lowly police work. However, at the corps level, there were military police squads that dealt with prosecuting crimes and processing information for possible prosecution. They were the ones who forwarded information to the military prosecutor's office. Therefore, at brigade level there was an MP unit that was dealing with these basic tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You've told us that it would be rather unrealistic to expect the security organ to be investigating itself or to be admitting to crimes it had committed, could you then -- would the possibility exist for you to go outside the military and, say, engage members of the civilian organs, such as the Ministry of Interior, to assist you in gathering information against members of the -- of the army, the security organ, for instance?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: According to the regulations that were in force, no, I did not have such a possibility. All I could do was, excuse me, to explain that the civilian police could perhaps have forwarded certain kind of information, but information in relation to things that had nothing to do with the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But couldn't you get them engaged to assist you in investigating, gathering information so that you could turn it over to the investigative judge so he could conduct his independent investigation as you indicated?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: As far as any involvement by the civilian police is concerned, if, for example, the prosecutor obtains certain information, this would possibly be within the competence of the civilian prosecutor because he has authority over the civilian police but not over the military police. This is something that the military prosecutor would not have the authority to do; not under the law, and it wasn't customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I failed to ask you earlier, could you on your own initiate the gathering of information for a potential investigation based on what you had heard? In other words, that there is no informant, there is no person coming to your office, but from the media you've heard that large-scale atrocities have occurred. Could you, on your own, initiate the gathering of information?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about me and my official position at the time, I did not have authority to gather any kind of information myself. I told you that back then I was working as the military prosecutor of the army of Republika Srpska and my job was to pursue appellate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So you as the chief prosecutor at that -- at the second instance had no competence of initiating investigations?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But let's assume that you, at the time, were the prosecutor at the first instance. You would have been able, surely based on the laws that existed and applied then, to initiate the gathering of information to see whether it should be forwarded -- suspects could be identified so that information could be forwarded to the investigative judge so he or she could conduct their investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I know that you were not the prosecutor at the first instance at that time, but can you tell us whether it would have been realistic for a prosecutor to commence an investigation based on information that he had learned against the security organ of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: De jure he would have had the right, but bearing in mind the situation that prevailed at the time, the seriousness of the crime, the level of the officer suspected in your hypothetical case of having committed the crime, I don't think he would have done it, bearing in mind that there was danger. His life would have been in danger, the lives of his family members, so I doubt that anyone would have done this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But de facto, how realistic would it have been? You told us de jure it was possible. I'm asking de facto.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Practically it would not have been realistic. As I've said, Prosecutors and judges had no physical protection. At the time, the prevailing mood in the country and in the army was such that anyone who attempted to do anything would have been demonised. Also, the persons suspected of having committed crimes were dangerous people, people who were ready to do anything, to remove people even physically. People were killed for other reasons and no criminals were ever discovered who had done this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally in these guidelines, if I can take you back to P380 before we move on, I just want to make sure I have it correct. When a report is filed, based on these guidelines, is it done by the commander personally or is it on behalf of the command unit?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: This was done on behalf of the command unit. Let me explain. I said that the commander had his assistant for security matters and the military police, and in the nature of things, they were supposed to collect information for a criminal report on their own and then deliver the document with the supporting materials to him for his signature. So he merely signed the document on behalf of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So in other words, these guidelines that we're speaking of, if they were to be applied, the commander of a brigade would be relying on the investigative work of his chief of security to provide him with the report, the evidence, and so forth in order to sign the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know it may sound silly, but how realistic would it have been for a commander of a brigade to really expect his chief of security to honestly and with integrity collect evidence if, in fact, that very same chief of security had been involved in committing the very same crimes for which the criminal report was being prepared, crimes that he had committed or was involved in, other members of the security organ from the corps and the Main Staff level? How realistic would that have been? And I don't want to hear about de jure. I want to know de facto.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I think we can move on to the next area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And perhaps, Your Honour, because of the area I'm moving on in or for other perhaps technical reasons, if we could take an early break. I don't have that much more, but I would like to -- it would be most helpful, let me put it that way, if we take an earlier break today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We are very flexible concerning the break in time, and we will resume at twenty minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Drinic, I want to switch now to another topic. Perhaps you can assist us. First of all, do you know a Mr. Gajic who was with the military police of the East Bosnian Corps in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday he testified under oath that during the period when he was with the military police, I believe it was the 3rd Battalion of the East Bosnian Corps, that between the period of 1992 and 1994, the period that he was in that unit, specifically in the investigative unit of the military police, that there had been cases, in fact several, he indicated, or numerous, where Serbs were being investigated for, and even tried and convicted, for crimes against Muslims. My question to you, sir, is you having been in Bijeljina, having been the prosecutor at the first instance level at least part of that time, could you please tell us whether that was, in fact, the case.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. There were cases where proceedings were initiated against Serbs where the victims were either Muslims or non-Serbs in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And are we specifically talking about war crimes or just crimes in general?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Crimes in general. Many of them were cases of murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know a Mr. Novak Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to read a portion of the transcript from yesterday, verbatim, questions that were posed by the Prosecution to Mr. Gajic, and perhaps you could assist us a little bit. And the question was posed, and I'm reading from the unofficial transcript, it would be page 28, line 22, and I apologise for not having a copy for the ELMO, I marked it up before I could make a copy, hence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, I think it's all right since you are going to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Right. But I just wanted to inform the usher because he seemed ready to -- to come and assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The usher is always ready to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know. Especially this particular usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, it states here: "Okay. Now, you're referring to the years between 1992 and 1994. I take it that those cases that you say took place." Answer: "Yes." Question --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now the question is this: "Do you know, sir, who Mr. Kovacevic is?" Mr. Gajic's answer is: "No, I'm not familiar with that person." Question: "You're not aware, sir, that he was -- he worked as a prosecutor in the Bijeljina district before 1992, subsequently became the chief prosecutor there and was sitting as a judge in the Bijeljina district?" And the answer is -- his answer, Mr. Gajic's answer is: "I was in touch with Prosecutors from the Bijeljina district but not with Mr. Kovacevic. Probably he had left the prosecutor's office by then."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would object on the basis that this is improper to read from the transcript from yesterday. If Mr. Karnavas has a question, he can just ask the question. If he has some predicates to that question, he can ask them, but there is no need to read verbatim from the transcript from yesterday. This is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the Defence counsel is laying the foundations for his question. The question will be followed up, and we believe this question concerns the credibility of the witnesses. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first of all, first and foremost, was Mr. Novak Kovacevic working as a prosecutor in the Bijeljina district before 1992, as Ms. Issa, the Prosecutor, would have us believe yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And incidentally, for the record, Mr. Kovacevic's response, which is consistent with Mr. Drinic's, can be found on page 6819. Can you please tell us where Mr. Kovacevic was working at the time, if you know, prior to 1992.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: He was working as a first instance civilian prosecutor, civil prosecutor, in the basic prosecutor's office in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Rogatica is not the Bijeljina district, is it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. No. It's after Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, for those of us who don't know the terrain, just to make sure. Now, in the -- between the period of 1992 and 1994, did he work as a prosecutor, as a military prosecutor, in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he work as a judge, a military judge, in Bijeljina from the period of 1992 to 1994, the period which concerns us with respect to Mr. Gajic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He didn't work as a military judge in Bijeljina either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know by chance where Mr. Kovacevic did in fact work during that period of time, 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: In 1992, he worked for a time as a first instance judge at the military court in Sarajevo. I don't know the exact date, but later on he worked as a judge at the supreme military court with its seat in Han Pijesak at the time. Later on it moved to Zvornik. That was when I joined the prosecutor's office there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did Mr. Kovacevic eventually become the chief prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, in the year 2000, starting on the 15th of March. He took my place when I went to civil prosecutor's office in the Bijeljina district.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again for the record, Mr. Kovacevic's work history can be found in his statement that he gave -- or his testimony given on the 28th January, 2004. Now, let me ask -- let me ask the next question that was posed to Mr. Gajic, and perhaps you can assist us with this one. The Prosecutor says, this is the question: "According to Mr. Kovacevic, sir, all the military records after the dissolution of the military court in 2000 were sent to the Bijeljina district, were transferred there, and that according to him" - that is Mr. Kovacevic - "there were no such records that reflected that the VRS was -- members of the VRS were prosecuted for committing crimes against Muslims. Are you aware of that?" That was the question posed to Mr. Gajic. And of course Mr. Gajic says in his answer: "I don't know what Mr. Kovacevic said, but I say this with full responsibility: I had two persons detained and carried out investigations with respect to Bijeljina municipality because they had committed the murder of two young Muslims, Bosniaks, on the River Drina," and it goes on. So my question now is while you were a prosecutor there, were any investigations, any trials carried out against Serbs for committing crimes against Muslims during the period 1992 and 1994, as Mr. Gajic would have us believe?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. Not only two cases. There were more than two for the crime of murder where the victims were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to dissect this question posed by Ms. Issa. She says that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. My colleague Ms. Issa is not on trial here. If Defence counsel has an appropriate question, he can ask the question. And we can see the danger here in reading extensively from the transcript: It's clearly leading and then the question comes up afterwards about the very subject that he's just been reading from the transcript about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond, because this has been sort of a hot issue. I have repeatedly argued the importance of being truthful with the -- and honest with the transcript. I have Mr. Kovacevic's statement here -- or transcript here, and it has been taken, one, out of context; and two, it has been misstated. Now, yesterday, because of the situation, I chose not to be my energetic self in objecting. However, I do believe that a prosecutor who stands up and quotes from a transcript or purports to paraphrase from the transcript should do so honestly and with integrity. Now, obviously she misspoke. I'm not suggesting anything evil or nefarious, but nonetheless she misspoke and it left us with the appearance that perhaps Mr. Gajic himself, the witness who testified under oath, was in fact being less than candid. Here I'm giving this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What's the problem? I don't understand the problem. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This court is not a forum for Mr. Karnavas to make personal attacks on the Prosecutor, especially the day afterward when the Prosecutor is no longer in the courtroom, especially in front of a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These are not personal attacks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if he has points to make that information was brought out that was incorrect from yesterday, he can bring that out through the witness and he can argue it, but to use this podium as a way to personally attack someone like this repeatedly is wrong, especially when the foundation for those attacks is flimsy, as we see it. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We don't see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- it's inappropriate, especially in front of a witness that we're trying to, you know, get information out of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will pose a question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I want to say a few words on this issue. First of all, I think yesterday you had plenty of opportunity to cross or redirect the witness on any issues raised by the prosecutor yesterday. Secondly, Mr. Karnavas, I don't know about the American legal system very well, but at least in my jurisdiction we pay special respect to the women colleagues. I think I have reminded many times that you should concentrate on your question rather than attacking the other parties, especially a woman colleague. This is a warning to you, Mr. Karnavas. I hope in your question you never mention the name of the Prosecutor, or use the commonly used terminology as "my learned colleague."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And lastly, Mr. Karnavas, I believe in this point there is no need to read the transcript again, just to put your question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. For the record, though, I do wish to file a formal complaint against the Prosecutor yesterday, because if you go to page 6820 to 6823 you will see that there was a mischaracterisation, a blatant mischaracterisation of the testimony of the witness, and I'm entitled to make my record. Now, there is no other way to challenge a Prosecutor who continually mischaracterises the record other than to go to the record itself. That's what I was attempting to do. I never made any personal attacks at all. An objection was raised. I'm entitled to respond. I'm responding to that objection. Now, I'm reading from the official transcript yesterday where she's saying certain things and I'm asking this gentleman to comment on it. That's all I'm doing. And then we can go to official transcript and you will see, Your Honour, that what Mr. Kovacevic said is different from what the Prosecutor alleges that he had said for the purposes of impeaching the witness. That's all. This is classic impeachment and I don't see it being personal in nature. And whether it's a woman or a man, Your Honour, it would be the same for me, but I don't see the distinction. We're all colleagues in court and all on equal footing, but I take your notice, and I will proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas has just in open court filed what I believe is an ethical complaint against an attorney in this office. He just said that, Your Honour. Now, you can -- you can read what's saying. "However, I wish to file a formal complaint about the Prosecutor yesterday, because if you go to page" such-and-such there was a mischaracterisation. This is a very, very serious allegation to be made in a court of law against any lawyer. Their word is their soul, is their reputation, is everything they are founded on, and to make what is a formal allegation, it needs to be followed up. If needs to be reviewed. It needs to be looked at. There are procedures and processes in this Tribunal to do such a thing. I think Mr. Karnavas was just talking and maybe he will withdraw his formal complaint and it's just a matter of frustration because of his view that she mischaracterised something, and if that's the case, we can all relax and go forward. Lawyers sometimes make inadvertent mischaracterisations or understand things differently, and I think we've seen that over and over again, and -- but if we are at a stage where formal complaints are being filed, we need to either start the process or just acknowledge it was just, you know, adversarial talk, because especially when we look at the subject matter that we're in today regarding formal processes and the importance of identifying misconduct and punishing it, this is something that is important. So if it's not anything, if it's just frustration from yesterday's and the viewpoint that she was mischaracterising, okay, let's go forward, but if it's more than that, I think that needs to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I hope you could think it over, and we might have an out of court meeting, say a 65 ter meeting or whatever, to solve those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And let me assure the Prosecution that I -- I made the comment in response to Your Honour's rather, in my opinion, harsh characterisation that somehow I'm attacking them personally. Lawyers do misspeak and do misquote the records on occasion. However, there are times when I think after a very long trial that lawyers particularly need to be careful, because sometimes they may give the impression that the witness is being less than candid on the stand. And so when pushed, I push back. So I certainly don't wish to -- to have anything proceeded against the Prosecutor, that particular Prosecutor we're speaking of, my learned colleague, as the Court would prefer me to address that person. But nonetheless, I would like to go forward at this point in time and clarify certain portions of the record so we have a clear understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Drinic, were all the military records of the military courts in 2002 when the court was dismantled or dissolved, were they all sent to Bijeljina district? In 2000. I'm sorry, not 2002 but 2000.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No, not all the military records of the military prosecutor's office were sent to the district court or the district prosecutor's office in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Where were they sent, sir? Was there one -- first of all, let me back up. Was there one collection point where all the records were sent to if you are aware?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. That's just what I was about to say. The records and files were sent on to regional authorities and distributed according to the respective competencies of the district courts and prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, for the Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik area, where were those records sent, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Some of those records were sent to the district court and district prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. And some of those records were sent to the district court and district prosecutor's office in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why -- why did -- were they not sent to one collection point?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: After the military judicial bodies were dismantled pursuant to a law, and I have in mind both the district courts and the district prosecutor's office, the records were divided into two levels in terms of their competence, who would be competent for them. The first instance district courts and prosecutors forwarded their files to their respective district courts and district prosecutors' offices. The district court would send on the documents to the court in Banja Luka; the one in Bijeljina sent their files to the district court in Bijeljina, and the military court and the military prosecutor's office in Bilici sent their files to the district court and district prosecutor's office in Trebinje. At that time, or rather, by that time, the military prosecutor's office and the military corps of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had already been dismantled, and the Zvornik Bratunac Srebrenica area had been under their jurisdiction back in 1995. Bearing in mind the breakdown of units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, pursuant to an order, they were sent towards Herzegovina and the East Bosnia Corps, the breakdown of the respective files and documents was done the same way; some went to Trebinje in Herzegovina and some of the files ended up in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just one last matter with respect to Mr. Gajic. He indicated that there should be some records with respect to those cases that he had worked on where indeed there had been a prosecution and a conviction. Could you please tell us if there were -- there was an interest in getting those documents to verify Mr. Gajic's testimony under oath, could you please tell us, where would one go to look for those records?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: These records could be obtained from the district court and district prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. All the files are available. I have personal knowledge of this, namely because investigators of The Hague Tribunal inspected all the files that they were interested in, and they even made copies of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that was my next topic. Have you had an opportunity to meet with the Office of the Prosecution, sir?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when that would have been, what year.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Right now I can't remember specifically if it was back in 2001 or possibly 2000. I really can't remember right now, but I know that I had been summoned by Mr. Trivun Jovicic who told me that the investigators would like to talk to me. So we agreed for me to give a statement, and I gave my statement in Zvornik at the OHR office. The interview went on for two days, and 12 audiotapes were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us what position you held when the Prosecutors came or members of the Prosecution office came to speak with you.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I was the deputy district civil prosecutor in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's where the records would -- would have been as well, or some of the records for that period; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during this two-day interview where you tell us some 12 audiotapes were recorded, could you please tell us whether there were any discussions about particular cases that had been investigated, perhaps even prosecuted, during the war of -- that is Serbs being prosecuted for crimes against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, we talked about that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: The investigators even put some documents to me from specific cases for me to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the Prosecutors themselves knew that there had been some cases of Serbs being prosecuted at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. It's inappropriate to comment on what the Prosecutors knew. If there's a question, he can simply ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it goes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think there is no problem with this question. It's quite logical to ask this question. You may move on, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you like to answer that question, sir. It would appear if the prosecutors presented you with documents regarding cases where investigations against Serbs having committed crimes against Muslims, that would appear that they were aware of such cases, would it not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's just what I said. I did not have a single document in my possession to support my statement. They were the ones who put certain documents to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you meet with any members of the Prosecution later?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the building of the district court and prosecutor's office. It was about 15 days or perhaps a month after I'd given my original statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the purpose for that second meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: During the original interview, they showed me a document where the OTP had initiated an investigation. However, in a strange way the investigation -- the criminal proceedings were dropped. At the same time, they showed me an indictment, which means that this specific person had been indicted. And it was on account of that they asked me, How is it possible that the prosecutor had dropped the charges and yet there is an indictment at the same time? I told them this was impossible, because if there was an indictment, there's no way any prosecutor could have dropped the charges previously. And since I was not familiar with the content of that specific document or file, I promised that I would do my best to inspect the specific file at the district court in Bijeljina. Sometime later, as I said, an investigator came back, and we inspected the file jointly. We inspected the investigations registry of the military court. There was not a single shred of paper that would have indicated that the prosecutor had dropped the case. However, the file contained this decision, this ruling by the judge that was being challenged, however, without the judge's signature. In actual fact, the accused was not, at the time, in detention but, rather, had left the country. How it was possible for something like this to happen, well, this is a question for the president of the military court, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that was a concrete case; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where were you able to get the documents in order to sit down with the investigator of the Office of the Prosecution of the Tribunal to go over it to try to solve this conundrum?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. The investigator came to see the president of the district court and requested a file from the Bijeljina military court as well as the file from the military prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. We were there together in the office of the president of the district court, and we went through those files. I wasn't there all the time, but the investigator even asked the president of the district court to have some of the files or portions of the files copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's move on to another topic, and I'm going to ask you concretely: Are you aware of any prosecutions or the initiation of any investigations as a result of incidents that occurred after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there was no concrete case that was initiated over that. I personally had an opportunity to attend a meeting at Zvornik, because a colleague of mine, my former boss from the Main Staff, had asked me to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we're going to -- we're going to speak about that particular meeting, but aside from that, I just want to get a concrete answer: Are you aware of any investigations or any cases being prosecuted for crimes that occurred against Muslims after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to hand you -- you said -- first of all, before I -- we go through the document itself, you indicated that at one point in time you attended a meeting. And could you please tell us a little bit about how it was that you attended this meeting, who was there, and what was the meeting about. I know it's a compound question, but it will save us -- me from asking it three different ways.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I went to that meeting by accident. I had received a fax from my former boss, who was the prosecutor of the army of Republika Srpska and who at the time was a legal officer attached to the Main Staff, telling me that pursuant to an order by President Karadzic, some data and information was to be verified concerning the Pilica village area. The meeting was to be attended by officials from the civilian police, civilian state security, military security, and officials from the Zvornik command. He in his capacity as a representative of the Main Staff could not attend the meeting. Therefore, since he was unable to make it there, he asked me to go and stand in for him at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go step-by-step. First of all, where was -- specifically, where was this meeting held, in whose office?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: The meeting was held in the office of the chief of the public security centre, Dragomir Vasic, in Zvornik, since the centre was based there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Vasic himself personally attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He presided over the meeting, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was a commission or -- established or was it being established as a result of this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I looked at the order itself, the order of President Karadzic, and as far as I could understand, he requested that a commission be set up to investigate a specific case, and I believe that those present made up the commission, or, rather, there was to be an agreement concerning a commission being set up. As I had not been officially invited to that meeting, I do not know what happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But having attended that meeting, was it your understanding that someone in particular was the -- the chairman of this commission or was going to be appointed the chairman of the commission? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After attending the meeting, did you by any chance generate any memoranda or any documents that would reflect the minutes of the meeting, at least as you understood them to be?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I didn't draw up any notes in the form of a memorandum, at least. I was given a sheet of paper to make some notes during that meeting; where the meeting was held, at what time, and who attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But after having attended the meeting, did you at least make a report? Since you were standing in for someone, for your superior, did you make a report and forward it onwards so at least one would have a record of, one, your attendance; and two, what you believe had transpired during that meeting in your presence?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you now what is P712, and you will be looking at P712B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I have to remind you that this document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I wasn't aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you could quote the paragraphs in this paragraph, but it would be better not to put all the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We don't need to put it on the ELMO, Your Honour. I just wanted to go through some aspects of it, at least to get him to comment without necessarily disclosing the full content.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could just look at this document, these documents, sir. Please look at them and go through them.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in these documents, I believe we have the one document, the order from President Karadzic; is that correct? If you go -- if you go backwards, forwards, looking at the last page, second last page, that would be the order from President Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in fact there's -- in that -- and the date on that, incidentally, was the 23rd of March, 1996; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then it would appear that there is a document dated 26 March 1996, and that bears your signature, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It says here "Major Predrag Drinic," so I take it you had a rank while you were a military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in this document, without going into the specifics, what -- if you can just tell us, what are you -- what are you trying to do? What is the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: As I said before, I was there by accident at this meeting. I had been asked to attend by a colleague of mine. Therefore, I was not invited. However, when I looked at the order by President Karadzic and what it was about, I realised that there were certain indications there that two bodies had been found that may have been the result of a crime. I attended the meeting, and out of all those present - I'm making no exception there - I found out that as for this information contained in the order, that there were two bodies that had been found in the Pilica area, that the people present knew nothing about that, which surprised me. I had assumed that the order by President Karadzic had been given based on reliable information. After all, he was at that time the state president. At the meeting, I obtained no information whatsoever. It was based on this order and the results of what transpired at the meeting that I wrote an official letter to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska intelligence and security sector in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Telling them to set up a commission and to verify the data on the spot. And then the results of their own investigation should be forwarded to the relevant military prosecutor or the relevant military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, would this be consistent with or similar to you as a prosecutor, if, say, you were at the first instance, making a request to the security organ for the collection of additional information?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's precisely what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So in essence, what you were doing is following the existing procedure at the time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I gave the initiative for the material collected by the security organ be submitted to the first instance military prosecutor and that the investigating judge of the military court be informed of this in order to possibly carry out an on-site inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During that meeting that you attended, do you know whether Mr. Vasic, who after all was the chief of the Zvornik security service centre, as I understand it is part of the Ministry of the Interior, in essence, he's the chief, he's the head of the police, for lack of a better term, did anyone task him in particular to see what, if any, information he could gather since, after all, Pilica was nearby Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I must tell you right away that I am not aware of this information. However, Zeljko Vasiljevic was from the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo. I don't know what they agreed, but he could have ordered Dragomir Vasic to look into this case because Pilica belonged to the public security centre in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you said that you were standing in but nonetheless we see that you generated a report that you forwarded upwards to the VRS Main Staff, the department of intelligence and security affairs. I take it that was to General Tolimir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: It would be better to say both to General Tolimir and to Colonel Beara. It was, in fact, Colonel Beara who was supposed to deal with this or, rather, his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you know what, if anything, happened as a result of your initiative, your proposal?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened. I never received any direct information as to whether anything had been done pursuant to this. For this reason, on the back of my letter which I sent, I drew up an official note, stating that I had received no reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that's your handwriting there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, it is. It is. It's my handwriting and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there is no dilemma about that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No dilemma at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
