utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if we could move on to the next document, and I want to show you Exhibit P713. You will be looking at 713B, which is in the original version. Now, do you recognise the signature at the bottom, sir?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this is dated 1 April 1996, and it would appear, would it not, sir, that the military prosecutor of the Republika Srpska army was served with this order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this means only that the document was to have been sent to the military prosecutor of the army of Republika Srpska. I assert with full responsibility that at that time I did not receive this document. I learned about this document because I saw a facsimile of this document in an independent newspaper in February 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to do step-by-step. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I believe we won't need your assistance any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you did not see this document, yet we see clearly that this was at least on the list of distribution of you -- your office was on the list of distribution. Could you please explain to us how it is that an order from the president himself, officially signed and stamped, how is it possible that such an important document would not have reached you? What is your explanation, if any?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have an explanation for it. At the time when this document was to have been sent, the law on military courts and of course the law on the military prosecutor's office provided for the de jure headquarters to be in Banja Luka. However, de facto, we were in Zvornik. I assume that the service which was supposed to deliver this document did not know about this and that in fact this order went to Banja Luka rather than to Zvornik. My assertion that we did not receive this I can support by the fact that there is no register or protocol in the military prosecutor's office of the army of Republika Srpska where this order has been registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that you became aware of this order at some point when this document appeared, or a facsimile of it appeared, in an independent newspaper in February 2000; correct? That was your testimony earlier.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, work with me on this one: From April 1, 1996 to February 2000, how is it that an order could be out there for such a long period of time and though you were not served with the order, how is it that you never became aware of its existence? Surely someone must have brought this to your attention, or somehow you would have learned it - how shall I put it? - at least through the grapevine or by rumour, somehow.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: As regards these facts and circumstances, you can observe that on this order, the prosecutor of the army of Republika Srpska is listed last. This means that in front of the military prosecutor of the army of Republika Srpska there were other people and other organs who had a greater responsibility to act on this. As far as I know, none of these acted on it, although in paragraph 3 of this order a request is made that everyone should take certain steps within their area of responsibility, and the coordination of all the organs listed here was requested. However, if someone had really taken any steps in connection with this order, I would have learned from one of these people listed here who were more important than I was and who would have been in charge of leading these activities, I would have been informed by them, but I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I just want to clarify one point because it sounds a little bit odd, shall I put it. You noted to us that you're listed at the bottom of the list, military prosecutor of the Republika Srpska. And in pointing that -- or bringing that to our attention, you would have us believe that somehow you were at the bottom of the list and therefore the least important organ within this list. How can you make such an assertion?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean to say literally that we were the least important organ but that there were organs who were supposed to take action before the prosecutor's office did. In a particular case, in the case of a particular crime and a suspect, we would get information from the security organ and the military police. When I say "we," I mean the military prosecutor. However, from this order it is evident that, according to the military structure, the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska is listed here, the Ministry of Defence, the supreme military court, so that according to this sequence, there were organs who were supposed to undertake certain action and take certain steps before the prosecutor's office did. In connection with this, I did not receive any information, and the information we have just been talking about regarding Pilica, well, I acted in accordance with my competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that if we were to look at that particular document, it would appear, at least from the date, that it was three days after President Karadzic's order, and I'm referring to P712. But getting back to this order, P713, I want to pose a hypothetical. Maybe you can help us out on this one. Let's assume that you had indeed received this order, that is it had been properly served on your office at your location, and that you had read this. What would have been the protocol? What would you have done under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I would have forwarded this order to two places. I would have forwarded it to the basic prosecutor or first instance prosecutor in Sarajevo, and I would have forwarded another copy of the order with a letter from me asking that this information be investigated to the organ for security and intelligence of the Main Staff, as I did in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. And perhaps I failed to ask you with respect in the previous case, that is Exhibit P712, the earlier one. Do you know whether your superior, the one that you had been standing in, whether he had received any information from the intelligence and security organ pursuant to your proposal?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. But in view of the fact that they were in the same place, it would be logical to conclude that their communication was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow that answer.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: My precise answer is that I do not know whether my former superior received any information from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, I want to move on beyond this document, 713, and just ask you, since you learned of it in the press in February 2000, that is three and a half years later, approximately three and a half years later, after learning of it, did you take any steps to come in -- to implement the order, albeit belatedly?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. This was precisely at the time when I had already been appointed deputy of the district public prosecutor, and I was no longer competent to take action. The time would have been too short, and the question would arise as to whether I was actually performing this duty at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, once you became aware of this order, did you take any steps at least to become aware of whether this order was being complied with by any of the above-mentioned or listed organs; the Main Staff, the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Justice, the Supreme Court, the supreme military court, the republic public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't take any action. But with hindsight, three years later I assume I would have known had they taken any action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you just a couple of general questions that I think might be relevant to you in particular. At some point in time after the fall of Srebrenica, more or less the entire world knew that atrocities had been committed. A large number of Muslim males were missing, their bodies unaccounted for. And then shortly thereafter, even mass graves were found. So clearly living in Bosnia and Herzegovina or the RS in particular, you would have become aware of what was being talked about in the press; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So certainly in light of your position, you would not have needed an order from the president to coax you into looking into these matters. So my question is: Did you or your colleagues at the military prosecutions office ever engage in any investigation or any investigative efforts to try to figure out who the suspects would be in order for a proper investigation through an investigative judge could commence?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, when I learned through the media that there was a possibility that some of the persons responsible or someone had committed a war crime, and with the names of high-ranking officers and politicians being mentioned, I could not believe this to be true. Because someone who issued orders that human rights conventions be respected, who issued orders saying that proceedings had to be initiated, I could not believe that these same people were perpetrators of war crimes. That was in the initial stage. A little later, I was able to learn, especially because I had information that in the area investigators from The Hague Tribunal had been active, I was informed that we were not to stand in their way or hinder them and that they would collect information on their own, independently. However, I received no specific information either about a person or about any specific war crime. So that it was not my job as a prosecutor in second instance, or appellate proceedings, to initiate an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Have you cooperated with the Office of the Prosecution to the extent that you have been requested to do so?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I received certain information about their activities. I was told not to hinder them. I didn't. But when they asked me to cooperate, to make a statement, I told you that I talked to them for two days, I gave them all the information I knew, and I drew their attention to certain documents I knew about. Besides this, we mentioned documents just a while ago, and as far as I was able to, in accordance with my information, I did start activities to collect information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it you would have been willing to come and testify on behalf of the Prosecution if they had called you as their witness?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, and I would have said the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it your testimony for them would have been the same as it has been for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Drinic, I want to thank you very much for coming here and giving us your testimony. I want to thank you for being frank and forthright. I believe the Prosecutor may have some questions, as well as the Judges. If you could be equally as forthright and candid with then as you have been with me, I would be most grateful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, I have no further questions on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Lukic, do you have any questions to put to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, our Defence does not have any questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, it's almost time for the break. We will break now and we will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination, Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours. Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Drinic.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for you here. Hopefully we won't keep you very long. Now, you testified during the direct examination that with regards to the crimes committed in the context of Srebrenica, July 1995, that as far as you know, there were no cases and no investigations conducted by any Republika Srpska authorities. Now, you were once the military prosecutor. This is something you would know about if you say something like that here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. My assertion was about the military judicial organs. I don't know about the civilian judicial organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, we heard a fair amount about what happened to various VRS -- I'm sorry, various military court or military prosecutor offices' records when they were transferred to civilian jurisdiction, but the result of those transfers, that doesn't change your answer, does it, whether the files went to Trebinje or Bijeljina, or wherever. Your answer would remain the same, wouldn't it, that there were no concrete cases and no investigations regarding the events in Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We just wanted to clarify that. You mentioned that you became aware through the media of allegations that there may have been crimes committed following the takeover of the Srebrenica enclave. Do you remember that and do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that you heard these media reports or when it was that, through the media, you learned of the allegations that criminal conduct had been involved?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Specifically, I learned that charges had been pressed before The Hague Tribunal against certain persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately what month or what year that was?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: It was quite a long time ago. I didn't keep a diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was before or after the jurisdiction went from the military courts to the civilian courts, the military courts being dissolved?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: That was before the military courts were dissolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So was that before or after the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: After the end of the war, bearing in mind the fact that the war ended in late 1995, once the Dayton Accords had been signed, and the events in Srebrenica took place in 1995, but in the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the transfer or dissolution of the military courts, that happened in spring or early summer of -- I'm sorry, spring or early summer of 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you hear about these allegations of crimes having occurred in Srebrenica July 1995, did you hear about that from any other sources apart from the media; perhaps some of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, with the exception of those documents, if those documents could be linked with the events in Srebrenica. I'm talking about Karadzic's order and the document that I sent to the Main Staff. However, at the time I couldn't be sure whether those bodies that had been discovered in Pilica were a result of the misdeeds that had been committed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So apart from these specific documents that you're just talking about now, the Karadzic order and a couple of the related documents, including one that you prepared, you didn't hear any allegations about crimes being committed in Srebrenica in July 1995? You didn't hear that from anybody else, from any other source? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Officially I didn't hear it from any other source.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, what about unofficially?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I told you I read about it in the papers or, rather, in the public media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But apart from that, no one -- you didn't hear from anybody or from any other source? You've explained the media. You've explained these documents. You didn't hear from anyone else or any other source allegations of criminal conduct Srebrenica July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. I mean, I have to answer by asking a question: Who would have been mad enough to familiarise a military prosecutor with a crime that had been committed, unofficially?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Drinic, could you tell us where you were living in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina. My family lived in Bijeljina. Monday to Friday I would stay in Zvornik, and over the weekend I would be with my family back in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you were staying Monday through Friday in Zvornik because that's where your office was located; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. And that's where I slept also.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, where -- where exactly in Zvornik was your office located?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: The office was on a street near the police headquarters, near the town hall municipality building, near the civilian first instance court or just adjacent to it, but withdrawn from the street, a bit behind, because there was another residential building just in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the address of that building where you worked was, having worked there for --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure about the address. I know that with the exception of the main street, all other streets are called St. Sava's street. I'm not sure about that one, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Where -- so that's where your office was. Where -- what was the address or where was it, if you could describe it to us, where you stayed in the evenings during the week.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. For a while I stayed at the Drina Hotel or, rather, I slept there, and then as my job there was reaching -- coming to an end, I slept in a room that was adjacent to the office in which I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So in July of 1995, does that mean, then, that you were staying at the Drina Hotel at that time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You say you think so. Was there anyone else -- anywhere else that you stayed apart from the Drina Hotel up until the time shortly before, as you say, you left your position?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No, no other place. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recall where you were during the days of the 10th, the 11th, the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: These are very specific dates, and it's been a long time, therefore, right now I can't remember. But if your reference is to the events that preceded the Srebrenica operation, what happened during the operation or just after the operation, I can give you my whereabouts, but please don't try to pin me down on specific dates or days since, frankly, I can't remember about specific dates, but I can give you my whereabouts if that's what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Can we -- let's take the day that Srebrenica fell. Could you tell us where you were on that day?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. The news about the fall of Srebrenica reached me over the TV, and I was in Ilidza, in the Serbia Hotel, because I had just arrived from Zvornik to Ilidza that very day to go to the first instance military court in Sarajevo and carry out a check there. When I say "Ilidza," I mean Sarajevo since that section of Sarajevo was Serb controlled at the time, Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When did you actually drive, if it's correct to say that you drove, when did you go from Zvornik to Ilidza and Sarajevo? What day? And if you can give us a day in relation to the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I wasn't the one who drove. There was a driver. But we left Zvornik and headed in the direction of Drinjaca, which is a major junction, and from there you go towards Vlasenica. If you look at a map, it's to the south, next to the River Drina. However, in Sveti Stefan or Divic, which is what the hamlet is called, the civilian police pulled us over and they told us that we couldn't drive straight through. They didn't give the reason. They said they had received orders not to let anyone through. The driver hailed from Zvornik, and he was familiar with a different road that we could take. Therefore, we took a route north of the village back towards Zvornik and then on to Bijeljina. We reached a junction in the village of Karakaj near Zvornik, and we set out for Tuzla, we took the road to Tuzla, because that was another road that you could take to reach Vlasenica. It was a roundabout way, and I can't remember the exact village -- exact villages that the road passes through. There again, we were stopped by the police. They told us that there were combat operations under way and that the road was not safe, but if we agreed to go at our own risk, we would be allowed to drive through. At the time, I didn't know what combat operations they were talking about, truth to tell. Had I known, maybe I would have refused to travel on, but I didn't know, and no one had informed me previously, not even my superior officer, and that would have been his duty, to inform me. I said that I wasn't afraid and that I felt perfectly fine travelling on for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So just to clarify, this was on the day that Srebrenica fell that you took this drive to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that. What I told you was that it was on that day, rather, that evening, that I heard in the TV news when I was at Ilidza that Srebrenica had fallen. I don't know exactly when Srebrenica fell, not to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What day did you drive back to Zvornik from Sarajevo? Just tell us the day, please, and you can tell us in reference to the day that Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I can tell you in relation to the day when I heard the news about the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: So I reached Srebrenica on that day -- sorry. I reached Ilidza. I heard the news. The next day - it was already late - I went out to carry out the check with the military prosecutor, and the next day after that, I headed back in the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a very specific question. We actually don't need to hear your entire itinerary or route on the way back on this one. On your way back to Zvornik, did you pass through Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you see soldiers there along the road?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Two days after the Srebrenica -- two days after Srebrenica was taken over, did you see any prisoners along the road?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't know when it was that Srebrenica fell. It's been a long time, and all I'm telling you is when I found out about the news that Srebrenica had fallen. And if you will please repeat the other half of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Drinic, I want to make this very clear if I haven't made it already: I am not asking you the day on which Srebrenica fell. I'm asking you when you went back in relation to the day Srebrenica fell. You remember that day. You explained to us it was two days later. Now, that's enough for us. I'm asking you whether you drove through Konjevic Polje. You said yes. I'm asking you when you were driving through Konjevic Polje, did you see any prisoners along the road or in the fields or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your answer is yes, you did see prisoners along the road?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, you are too fast. You have to make a pause and let the interpreter get across --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm happy to repeat that question, and I will slow down, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I want the record to reflect that there was no answer yes on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for this issue, I believe -- I believe Mr. Shin will follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Drinic, I apologise for that. I was speaking too quickly for the interpreters to catch up, so I will repeat my question. On your way through Konjevic Polje and on your way back to Zvornik, did you see any Muslim prisoners along the road, in the fields, or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I saw groups of soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska but no prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you went -- you went back to Zvornik on that day, and the same day you left Sarajevo you arrived in Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you continued working at your office in Zvornik after that for the next few days?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: During those days in Zvornik, those, let's say, two or three days following your return, were you aware of any Muslim prisoners being bused through Zvornik? There were thousands being bused through; we've had evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of a single bus or truck, not that I could notice any buses or trucks driving through, transporting those prisoners. This is something that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to another topic here. I'm going to refer now to a letter that you were shown earlier. This is Prosecution 713.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If that could be provided to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I just have just a simple question on this. Now, this is the letter that I think -- I believe you testified that you saw in a newspaper in February 2000 or thereabouts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And even though it's addressed to the military prosecutor, you explained -- your explanation about why it didn't reach you was that the Main Staff was de jure in Banja Luka but de facto in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I think you're making an error there. Not the Main Staff. The supreme military court and military prosecutor's office of Republika Srpska, which I was part of. That's this last portion. That's correct. The Main Staff remained where it was, in Han Pijesak, both de facto and de jure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I misspoke there. Thank you for correcting that. So it was the military court was de jure in Banja Luka but de facto in Zvornik. And that's your explanation about how this letter didn't get to you. Do you think this was a fact that wasn't known to the people delivering mail from the president to the military court? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe he's saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe first of all the gentleman was shaking his head, so at least we need to get a record of what he was stating; and number two, I believe we're jumping to some conclusions. He is misstating the evidence. The gentleman never made that assumption nor is he insinuating that. So I'm raising my objection on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the witness could answer that question by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, but perhaps Mr. Shin could repeat the previous question because the gentleman was shaking his head and it wasn't picked up on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Drinic, we just clarified that it was the military court that was de jure in Banja Luka and de facto in Zvornik. During your direct testimony, you explained that this -- that this difference between the de jure and de facto location of the military court explains why the -- this document did not get to you. Did I get that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: What I said is that that was an assumption of mine. It is no assertion, it is merely an assumption. It is a possible explanation that I can provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in order for this assumption or possible explanation to actually be the reason, it would have to be because people delivering mail from the president of the Republika Srpska to the military court didn't know about the difference between this de jure and de facto location; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that those are simple administrators, the couriers, they were not necessarily aware of that. You don't get the state president delivering -- well, the state president knows, of course, but what his errand boys know or don't know I really have no idea. They don't necessarily have to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's turn to another one of these documents. This is a document under seal, so if we could just have it personally provided to the witness and not placed on the ELMO, please. This is Prosecution 712. And I'm sorry, actually, before we move on to that, can I just ask you one other question about the previous document. There was some discussion during your direct examination about the addressees listed there on the previous document - that's Prosecution 713 - and the fact that the military prosecutor is listed last. My question for you is simply: Isn't it true that all the addressees on that document in fact have different responsibilities and different tasks, generally speaking, and also in relation to that kind of letter?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Everyone had different responsibilities and tasks. You're quite right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you had said that if anyone -- if someone had taken a step or taken some action in response to that letter, you would have been informed of it. I believe those are your exact words, actually. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: What I said is probably I would have been informed. I can't make an assertion there. I can't know for sure what some other people may or may not have done, Whether they would have informed me or not. What I said was I assume I would have been informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to show you another document. This is Prosecution Exhibit 714. This is a document of the Republika Srpska Ministry of Internal Affairs. It says at the top of it in English, it says "Reports." It's a two-page document, and in the B/C/S it's a three-page document, and I'd like you to look at the second page, at the top of which it says "Informacija." If you could please take a moment to look at that. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No, not before. This is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you could please just go ahead and take a minute to look through that document, and you can signal when you've had a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Frankly, as I said, I have never received this document through any official channels, nor was I aware of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I could please interrupt you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could please have this document on the ELMO. This one is not under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Drinic. Okay, Mr. Drinic, if you could please continue.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the simple reason why I'm saying this, I can see the name of the sender and I can see the recipient, the Republic, Ministry of the Interior, the minister's cabinet is sending this to the Ministry of Justice administration, Mr. Goran Neskovic. I don't know. Maybe there was a document written in a different form. It's been a long time, but I don't think I've ever seen a document like this before, and I don't know what my relation would have been to a document like this. It wasn't addressed to me. It wasn't even addressed to the prosecutor's office. Not even to a first instance court. It says Ministry of Justice and Administration. I really have no idea. Why do you think that I should have seen this document earlier? What leads you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Drinic, I was simply asking you. Now you have explained that you have not seen this earlier. That's fine. Looking at this document now, doesn't it appear to you that this document -- it appears that it's a response to a request to look into crimes committed after the takeover of Srebrenica, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: May I have a little time just to read it, please, because the text is quite extensive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If the usher could please move the document up a little bit so the entire document might be read by those viewing, and the Judges, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I've managed to get the gist of it. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This document is dated the 23rd of September, 1996; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Would you agree that this document appears -- appears to be a response to a request for more information about the events following the takeover of Srebrenica in July 1995, and in particular, events relating to the killings? And you'll see at the top there's a reference to mass killings among the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to -- I will object to this line of questioning unless the foundation can be established. We can all read the document and draw our own conclusions. We don't need somebody from Bijeljina to come over here, a former military prosecutor. Now, the gentleman indicated that he hasn't seen this document, nor was the document addressed to him. So if I could have some linkage as to why we need to go into this particular document with this particular witness to elicit this particular conclusion, then I'll sit down, but until then, I have to raise my objection, because I don't believe the gentleman has indicated that he has any basis from which he could offer an opinion other than from reading, digesting, and interpreting, all of which we can do on our own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, although the witness said that he did not see this document before, some facts in that document could be denied or confirmed by this witness. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's my dilemma, too, Your Honour. I don't know. So I would like to know what the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe the Prosecution in the cross-examination could ask some questions on the basis of documents and the witness has the total freedom, you know, to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Whatever answers, we'll accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Drinic, I'll repeat the question, but if you don't know, of course, you can simply say that. Does this document not appear to be a response to that order from President Karadzic that you had earlier seen?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions on that document. Mr. Drinic, I'd just like to take you back now to something you said earlier today in the direct examination, and I'm going to read back to you the question and the answer first so that we're clear on where we're beginning with. You were asked by counsel for the Defence, and I'm referring to a time line that says 9.28 on this transcript, although it may be a little later. The question: "Keeping in mind the environment at the time, and we're going back now to July 1995 and onwards, but 1995, 1996, that period, could you please tell us, how realistic would it have been for anyone, let alone a commander of a brigade, for instance, to initiate a criminal complaint requesting the Prosecution to gather information with respect to atrocities that might have been committed or were committed by members of the security organ that go as high Beara himself?" Your answer was: "In principle, de jure, that would have been possible. However, in view of the kind of environment that we were surrounded by and the atmosphere, the feelings of the citizens, the soldiers, the army officers, this would not have been realistic." I just wanted to ask you a few questions to follow up on your answer there. Now, when you were explaining the kind of environment that existed at that time, was part of the reason -- wasn't part of the reason for this environment that there preceded some -- preceded the events in July 1995 some three years of war in which many, many Serbs - civilians and soldiers - had lost friends and families killed by Muslims? Wasn't that part of what contributed to that environment that you speak of?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I can share your conclusion as it stands. It's well known, though, that anyone engaged in a war is not impartial. Why would they otherwise be waging war?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Drinic, you were speaking of the kind of environment that you said "we were surrounded by," and an atmosphere, and you were speaking about the feelings of the citizens, not just the soldiers, but also the feelings of the soldiers and the army officers. Wouldn't it be fair to say that these feelings that you're speaking of was contributed in part by the fact that there were people who had lost friends and family who had been killed by Muslims? I mean, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases where some soldiers, or better to say citizens, had had family members killed. I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's why you mentioned the feelings of citizens when you were talking about the environment and the atmosphere that existed in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Among other things, that was one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Of course, among other things as well. Now, you had explained that in this environment, realistically one couldn't really prosecute crimes committed by the security organs; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I did not understand your question. Would you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You were asked about the environment within which these crimes had occurred, and you explained that it was -- it was the environment that you explained, you described, that existed at that time that made it difficult or nearly impossible, if not impossible, to properly investigate and prosecute crimes committed by -- or the crimes that were committed in July 1995 following the takeover of Srebrenica. Do you recall explaining that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: In essence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This contributed to the difficulty in prosecuting or investigating crimes committed by, among others, the security organs, the military police. You talked about that at some length; right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I did, but your interpretation of my testimony is something I cannot understand because it's so long. If you ask me a specific question, I will be happy to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, let's just -- let's just move on to this question: Despite this atmosphere that you described, this environment that made such investigation and prosecution difficult, the Geneva Conventions were still in force in the Republika Srpska in July 1995, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Geneva Conventions were in force from the very beginning of the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because regardless of any individual orders issued by President Karadzic, the Main Staff, and the guidelines we had - I cannot recall the exact date but I think it was in 1992 - a constitutional law was enacted. In other words, the Assembly of Republika Srpska adopted a law adopting all the laws of the former SFRY, including all the conventions that were not contrary to the constitution of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just one final document I'd like to show you. This is -- has been marked for identification Prosecution Exhibit 867. It's a document entitled "Law on the Mandatory Reporting of Crimes Against Humanity and International Law," and it comes from the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska dated 31st December 1994. Mr. Drinic, are you familiar with this law, given the significance of its nature?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing in dispute about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd just like to turn your attention to Article 3. If you could please take a moment to locate that. And I'll read the entirety of that Article, Article 3: "If a person acting in accordance with Article 1 of this Law --" Article 1 refers to the reporting of violations of crimes -- I'm sorry, commission of crimes against humanity and international law, if such a person "wishes to have the public excluded from the procedure of making information or evidence mentioned in Article 1 paragraph 1 of this law available for inspection or delivery or from the procedure of testifying, the competent body entrusted with collecting information on crimes against humanity and international law shall guarantee the confidentiality of the procedure."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Where is this written down? Would you please tell me, because I have it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That would be on -- in Serbian it would be on the page marked with the number at the top 00874061. In the right-hand column you have paragraphs 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 at the bottom. So on the basis of that, there were -- it was possible to take some measures to ensure the confidentiality of proceedings, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. I have a different interpretation which I'm sure is more correct than yours, and I can explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Law on Criminal Procedure, and a part of this provision can be found in the law on military courts, having in view their special nature, the confidentiality of the procedure means that during the proceedings before the Court if there is a military secret or a state secret or a need to protect the morality of a person, the public can be excluded. This does not mean that the organs engaged in investigating, prosecuting, the military court or any other court would conceal certain documents from each other or from themselves. It would only be concealed from the general public. The public would not be able to follow the proceedings. Or in the judgement, and this is characteristic of proceedings against juveniles, the full name of the juvenile cannot be mentioned but only their initials. That is the essence of this. Because, to explain it further, how could a security organ or the police or, generally speaking, the persons who are supposed to discover the particulars of a crime, how could they be denied the information as to what persons these are?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I think that answers my questions. Thank you, Mr. Drinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm afraid there is a little bit, Your Honour, but not a whole lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were asked to focus on Article 3. If we could go to Article 1, and just keeping in mind the answer that you gave us, which was rather comprehensive, it says here: "Anyone in possession of information," and if we go down, it says, "is obliged to make such information or evidence available for inspection and, if necessary, deliver it to the competent body entrusted with collecting information on crimes against humanity and international law." Okay. Do you see that? I didn't read the entire first Article, but in looking at this, does it not state that the person who has possession of this information has to give it to you and -- correct? You would be the competent body; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: I think the competent body would mainly be the police or the security organ. Exceptionally it could be submitted directly to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we went down to Article 3, we would see again that this -- if you read Article 3 correctly, it would appear, would it not, that the competent body is not the one that is excluded from that information but, rather, the public; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And incidentally, just so there's no misunderstanding, this -- this law that was shown to you, is it not, sir, in conformity with your testimony on direct, the way you've described it to us?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know why this law was enacted at all. When one learns of a crime, there is a duty that is binding on all citizens. In some cases, in case of very serious crimes, even the relatives of the suspect are duty-bound to report the crime, not just the citizens at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to touch on a couple of matters. First of all, you were asked about the address of the -- where your offices were in Zvornik when you were in the military prosecutor's office. Now, first of all, as I understand your testimony on direct, when you were questioned for over two days or -- two days, for a period of two days, that questioning took place at the office of the High Representative in Zvornik itself, did it not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The office is located in the Drina Hotel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, had the prosecutor, had they expressed an interest at that point in time, or even after, that is prior to you coming here today, in wanting to know the exact address of your office, would you have been willing to show them where that office was located?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I would have shown them. I'm not sure, but I think I even told them where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So it wasn't sort of a military secret that you would have to get clearance from some commission in order to disclose and point out the building and say, "This is where my office was"?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: It's not a secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were asked about, and the testimony was, according to the Prosecutor, that there was testimony in this court - and we'll have to accept him at his word - that thousands of prisoners went through Zvornik. Through Zvornik. Now, first of all, the town of Zvornik, is it on the road or is it off the road? And the road I'm speaking about is the one from Bijeljina towards Konjevic Polje, that stretch.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: A part of Zvornik is on the road, and the road runs along the Drina River itself. So there are buildings close to the road. The rest of Zvornik is away from the road and the road cannot be seen from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Would somebody need to drive through Zvornik in order to continue on to go to Bijeljina, or if they wanted to go in that direction in Bijeljina, or could they just stay on the highway, such as it is?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need at all to enter Zvornik. That's why the road was built as a highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And this road that I'm calling a highway, it's actually one lane in one direction and one lane in another direction with the Drina River on the one side and Zvornik being on the other; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's just how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So somebody could drive all the way from Konjevic Polje to Bijeljina, and if they wanted to stop in Pilica or Branjevo farm without ever going through Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: They wouldn't have to go through Zvornik if they took the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. One last question: You were asked a question about the Geneva Conventions being in effect at the point in time. My question to you is quite simple: A prosecutor at the basic level, the first instance, do you think it would be possible for them to recite the Geneva Conventions as a protection against members of the security organs whom the prosecutor would be investigating for serious crimes? Do you think that would be sufficient protection in light of the fact that no other protection was being afforded to them, that is physical protection?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG DRINIC
utterances.text: Whatever they had written, whichever authority they had referred to, right there on the spot with no one there to protect them, with no one else to back the proceedings, the opening of a case, there was nothing they could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no -- no further redirect, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Well, at this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The law marked Prosecution Exhibit 867, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This document P867 is admitted into evidence. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room, and we wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to my understanding, this is the last witness for this week. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Potentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: "Potentially." What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was that one witness, Your Honour, that we had been trying to bring over here, and a subpoena was issued. It's my understanding that there is a very, very slight possibility, although I doubt it, we would have heard by now, that this gentleman could arrive as early as, you know, Friday to testify, but that's why I say "potentially," because I always leave myself a little room. But I would suspect the answer to that question is yes, that's it for this week. We do have two other witnesses next week. And this gentleman, if he does indeed arrive, we will try to squeeze him in-between. So we expect it would be Witness 42, for this witness to testify on or about Wednesday. Now, since I'm on the floor, with respect to this issue of witnesses next week, the last witness is a rather significant witness, and try as I might to bring the witness earlier, and in light of the efforts that had to be made by everyone, we -- a certain amount of flexibility had to be shown, so we were locked into two particular days only, and I didn't wish to push the matter and force the situation. So I would respectfully request that if it is at all possible for the -- next week Thursday, Friday, that we go full days, full days, if possible, at least on Thursday, because then -- because I would certainly like to end on time, on the targeted date, as we've indicated. So I believe my direct could be -- I don't believe it's less than a day - probably more, in fact - and I certainly want to give the Prosecution adequate time to ask their -- for them to ask their questions, so I would like two full days next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, on this matter I think I have to consult with the Registrar to see the time schedule for the next week. And I don't think this Bench will -- will complain about the delay of your case. I believe that you conduct your case very smoothly, generally speaking, according to the schedule, which means that you finished your case before the deadline set by this Trial Chamber. But still, there are some witnesses left over, especially, you know, this Bench has not made any decisions concerning the 92 bis witnesses, and we might, we might call, if necessary, some of those witnesses for the live testimony after the 25th of this month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As I understand that, Mr. Jokic's case will begin officially on the 7th of July, and they also promised us that they could finish their case before the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We would be delighted to have any additional witnesses come. I did speak with Mr. McCloskey a little bit on this issue, and I understand -- and I don't want to speak for him, but I understand that he was going to also look at those lists of witnesses and perhaps we might have some readjustment to their position, and we certainly are willing to work with them to the extent that we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any matters on your part, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, but I don't anticipate a very long cross-examination of -- I believe we're talking about Colonel Karremans, and so we can work that into the schedule. But I -- as you know, it's hard to anticipate perfectly, but I don't see us having to spend more than a session or so with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- but as for this Trial Chamber, we'll do our best to accommodate the request from the Defence. We want them to have enough time to do their direct examination. At the same time, I have to remind the parties that this witness is somehow a little bit sensitive, you know, in the Netherlands, and which may, you know, touch upon some critical issues, local political, you know, matters. This is what we don't want. So as a piece of advice, I would like to tell the parties to not go into that deep which is outside the scope of our case. Secondly, pay some respect to all the witnesses, especially this one. This is the initial advice I would like to offer to the parties during their direct examination and the cross-examination. Well, having said that, I think the hearing for today is adjourned.
